source.text: ובכן ראיתי רשעים קברים ובאו וממקום קדוש יהלכו וישתבחו בעיר אשר כן עשו גם זה הבל־־׃
source.note: Unpointed editorial composite: normalized WLC8:10 with וישתכחו changed to וישתבחו, a bet reading reported by De Rossi's Hebrew collation. This is not verbatim WLC, a fresh glyph reading or a recovered autograph; exact original pointing and historical priority are unresolved. All other normalized consonants and encoded punctuation retained.

apparatus.note: Original/corrected/uncertain reports and kaf marginalqere in Kennicott553/DeRossi331 distinguished; no independent manuscript-count vote.

apparatus.witness: Selected Rahlfs-Hanhart/Swete Greek and Weber-Gryson Latin
apparatus.note: Passive praise in versions; not automatic proof of Hebrew reflexive boast or exact source letters.

translation.text: And so I saw the wicked buried; they had come and gone from the holy place[a], and had boasted[b] in the city where they had done so. This too is vanity.[c]

footnotes.text: “The holy place” may refer to the temple precincts or another sacred place.

Unapplied alternative: a Hebrew bet reading reported in manuscript collations is interpreted here as “had boasted”; Greek and Latin instead express “were praised.” The Masoretic Hebrew and consulted Syriac and Targum texts express forgetting. The exact earliest wording, subject and timing remain uncertain.
Hebrew hebel, traditionally rendered “vanity”; it can also mean “vapor,” suggesting something fleeting or elusive.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Introduces an observation/conclusion from the preceding reflection. 'And so' preserves both the connective waw and the inferential force of בכן in natural English.
Simple past fits Qoheleth's report of observation in context.
Standard rendering that preserves the moral category without unnecessary expansion.
Passive participle used predicatively after 'I saw'; 'buried' is the most concise natural English rendering.

Taken with the following verb as part of a sequence describing the wicked's prior activity. 'Had come' smooths the relation to the subsequent 'gone' in English. The verb can mean 'come/enter'; context suggests movement associated with the holy place.
מקום קדוש is most naturally 'holy place.' The phrase likely refers to a sacred precinct, but 'sanctuary' is slightly more interpretive, so 'holy place' better preserves the Hebrew wording.
הלך often means 'go/walk.' In this sequence, English idiom favors 'come and gone,' capturing repeated or completed movement without woodenly preserving 'walk.'

alternatives: were praised (passive versional wording or another analysis)
lexical_decisions.lexicon: BDB transcription of שבח and actual source comparison; no fresh HALOT consultation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical bet/hitpael alternative permits a reflexive boast interpretation. Had places boasting in the prior activity already expressed by had come and gone, rather than making buried people boast after death. It does not certify this temporal interpretation or make Greek passive praise identical to Hebrew reflexive grammar.
The article points to a definite city in the scene envisioned by Qoheleth.

alternatives: where they had done these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Hebrew is somewhat compressed. 'Done so' preserves the anaphoric force of כן without over-specifying the referent. 'Where' follows the relative construction with בעיר naturally in English.
Ecclesiastes' recurring הבל is traditionally rendered 'vanity'; while 'vapor' is more concrete, 'vanity' remains idiomatic and captures the book's refrain in readable English.
